identity: A school Arabic-language textbook page teaching the spelling of الألف المقصورة. It has a title line, a short didactic children's poem in which the maqsura alif speaks in the first person and argues with الألف الممدودة about which of them comes first, six interleaved rhyming rows of example words that carry the letter (verbs رمى كفى سعى شفى طوى روى نوى لوى بغى ضحى, nouns ندى مدى هوى لدى المرعى المستشفى, particles حتى بلى إلى على), a small narrative stanza about ليلى and الوردة, and a closing prose exercise instruction addressed to the pupils. Genre = verse plus workbook, with exactly one prose instruction block at the very end.
law: Native unit = the printed line, and this format shows me the printed lines directly as <NL>. In the verse body every line is one metrical unit (~9-10 syllables) and one segment, so the 26 line-final anchors plus the final token carry essentially the whole segmentation; enjambment across the line breaks proves the boundaries here are line-driven rather than syntax-driven, so I do not subdivide a verse line except where one independent clause is simply juxtaposed to another. Inside the example rows the و is bare-word و and never cuts (conjunct-weight test). In the single closing prose paragraph the ordinary corpus law resumes: one finite predication per unit, و plus its own predication cuts, و plus a bare noun does not, a setup that promises content ends its own unit, and a tight subordinator (أن, and the ثم that sits inside its complement) never opens a unit.
reasoning: HARD SITES. (1) The verse body as a whole. The poem is enjambed across the line breaks: الوردة قالت لي أخشى / في الشرفة أن أبقى عطشى, and جاءتني الألف المقصوره / تطلب أن تظهر في الصوره, and المقصورة جاءت زحفا / تسأل عن حالتها لهفى. In each pair the mandatory boundary falls in the middle of one grammatical sentence, which tells me the segmentation of this document is line-driven, not syntax-driven. So the 26 line-final anchors plus the final token are the backbone and I add almost nothing inside them. (2) The six example rows: ك رمى و كفى و سعى و شفى ; و ندى و مدى و هوى و لدى ; و ردى و شوى و سدى و عوى ; ك طوى و روى و نوى و لوى ; و بغى و ضحى و وغى و رحى ; حتى و بلى و إلى و على. These tempt me hard toward the word-drill law (one printed word = one unit), which is the single longest run of misses in my record. I reject it here for four reasons: the connectives are bare-word و, each conjunct being one word with no predication and no material of its own, which is the explicit no-cut side of the conjunct-weight test (compare السمع والبصر والشم والذوق واللمس kept whole); a real drill list is asyndetic, this one is syndetic; these rows scan and rhyme exactly like the surrounding verse lines and are metrically integrated into the poem; and each row is headed by ك (such as) or continues that ك, so the items are exemplification riding inside one phrase, not exchangeable answer-siblings. No cuts inside any of the six rows. (3) أين تراني أين مكاني at ⟨22⟩-⟨25⟩, the only verse line holding two independent juxtaposed clauses. Against a cut: metrically it is a single ~10-syllable line just like its neighbours, not a bayt of two hemistichs (its neighbours جاءتني الألف المقصوره and في آخر حرف تلقاني cannot be halved), and repeating the same question can be intensifying apposition rather than enumeration. For a cut: it is asyndetic clause plus asyndetic clause, a repeated opening word (أين … أين) is a repeated boundary in this corpus, a question is its own unit, and nothing protects a bare asyndetic clause however short. My calibrated bias is 7:1 toward merging, and the two readings are otherwise even, so I take the cut at ⟨23⟩ and mark it lo. (4) Speech verbs: ومضت تنشد عملي أحلى, الوردة قالت لي أخشى, قالت درسك حقا كفى. Quoted content stays attached to its speech verb, so no cut after تنشد or قالت even though the source almost certainly had a colon or quotation marks there. (5) بل كفى في الشرح ووفى at ⟨144⟩-⟨148⟩: ووفى is a bare verb with no complement of its own riding on the same subject, and a بل-correction absorbs its own و-continuation. No cut. (6) The closing prose block ⟨150⟩-⟨173⟩ is the only genuine prose, with no <NL> inside it, and it holds three predications. I cut before نطلب at ⟨153⟩: في القصيدة ألفات مقصورة is a complete existential predication that sets something up, and نطلب منكم … brings a new agent and a new speech act (an instruction), which is the setup-then-content shape of the announcer family, and asyndetic finite clauses cut by default outside the big-unit genres. The competing reading, that نطلب منكم أن تجدوها is an asyndetic sifa on the indefinite ألفات مقصورة (alifs that we ask you to find), is real, and it is why this is med rather than hi. I do NOT cut at ثم ⟨158⟩, even though ثم cuts everywhere else in my record, because تجدوها and ترتبوها are both subjunctive under one أن: they are one governed complement of one request, and a cut would strand a dependent fragment. I DO cut before والمجتهدون at ⟨165⟩: في الحروف والأسماء والأفعال is a run of bare nouns whose و never cuts, and then the very next و carries a new subject, a new finite verb, future tense and its own object. Same particle, opposite verdicts, inside one sentence, decided purely by conjunct weight. It also advances rather than comments: it stops instructing and starts predicting something about a subset of the readers. That one is hi.
